title: Ray (Geometric) Optics & Optical Instruments
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Reflection, Spherical Mirrors, Snell's Law, Total Internal Reflection (TIR), Refraction at Curved Surfaces, Lens Maker's Formula, Prism Deviation, Optical Instruments (Microscopes & Telescopes)
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: When Can Light Be Treated as a Straight Line?

In Chapter 21, we saw that light is an electromagnetic wave with wavelengths ranging from $400\text{ nm}$ to $700\text{ nm}$. If light is a wave, why do we draw straight lines (rays) and use geometry in mirrors and lenses?

The answer lies in the obstacle size: Whenever the size of mirrors, lenses, and apertures is very large compared to the wavelength of light ($\lambda \ll D$), wave diffraction effects become negligible, and light energy travels along rectilinear paths called light rays. This simplification is called Geometric or Ray Optics.

The Sign Convention Rules (Cartesian Coordinate System):
  1. All distances are measured starting from the Pole (for mirrors) or Optical Center (for lenses) as the origin $(0,0)$.
  2. The incident light ray ALWAYS travels from left to right. Distances measured along the direction of incident light are positive ($+$); distances measured against the incident light are negative ($-$).
  3. Heights measured above the principal axis are positive ($+$); heights measured below are negative ($-$).

topics.title: Laws of Reflection, Spherical Mirrors, Mirror Formula, Magnification & Velocity of Image
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Spherical Mirror Formula & Magnification
$$\text{Mirror Formula:} \quad \boxed{\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}} \qquad \left(\text{Focal Length } f = \frac{R}{2} \text{ for both concave and convex mirrors}\right)$$
$$\text{Transverse (Lateral) Magnification } (m): \quad \boxed{m = \frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v}{u} = \frac{f}{f - u} = \frac{f - v}{f}}$$
  • Concave Mirror: $f < 0$, $R < 0$. Real images have $m < 0$ (inverted); virtual images have $m > 0$ (erect).
  • Convex Mirror: $f > 0$, $R > 0$. Always forms diminished, virtual, erect images ($0 < m < 1$).
1.2 Velocity of Image for Moving Objects

1. Longitudinal (Axial) Velocity of Image (Object moving along principal axis):
Differentiating $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$ with respect to time $t$ gives $\frac{dv}{dt} = -\left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^2 \frac{du}{dt}$:

$$\boxed{v_{\text{image/mirror}} = -m^2 \times v_{\text{object/mirror}}}$$

2. Transverse Velocity (Object moving perpendicular to principal axis): $v_{iy} = -m \cdot v_{oy}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Mirror Formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u

Consider a concave mirror with pole $P$, focus $F$, and center of curvature $C$. For a paraxial ray making small angles with the principal axis, geometry of similar triangles yields $\frac{-u - (-f)}{-f} = \frac{-f}{-v - (-f)} \implies \frac{u - f}{f} = \frac{f}{v - f} \implies (u-f)(v-f) = f^2 \implies uv - uf - vf + f^2 = f^2$. Dividing by $uvf$ gives $\boxed{\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}}$!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Longitudinal Magnification $m_L$ for Finite Objects): While infinitesimal axial length has $m_L = -m^2$, for a finite object of length $L$ placed along the axis between $u_1$ and $u_2$, the exact image length is $\Delta v = |v_2 - v_1|$ (do not blindly use $m^2 L$ unless the object is extremely small!).

topics.title: Refraction at Plane Surfaces, Snell's Law, Apparent Depth, Total Internal Reflection (TIR) & Critical Angle
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Snell's Law of Refraction & Apparent Depth
$$\text{Snell's Law:} \quad \boxed{\mu_1 \sin i = \mu_2 \sin r \iff \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} = {}^{1}\mu_2 = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}}$$
Apparent Depth ($h_{\text{apparent}}$) in a Denser Medium (Refractive Index $\mu$):
If an object at the bottom of a pond of depth $h$ is viewed vertically from above in air ($\mu_{\text{air}} = 1$):
$$\boxed{h_{\text{apparent}} = \frac{h_{\text{real}}}{\mu}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Apparent Shift:} \quad \Delta h = h_{\text{real}} - h_{\text{apparent}} = h_{\text{real}}\left(1 - \frac{1}{\mu}\right)$$

If viewed through multiple stacked layers of liquids of thicknesses $h_1, h_2, \dots$ and refractive indices $\mu_1, \mu_2, \dots$: $\boxed{h_{\text{app}} = \frac{h_1}{\mu_1} + \frac{h_2}{\mu_2} + \dots}$.

1.2 Total Internal Reflection (TIR) & Critical Angle ($\theta_c$)
$$\text{Critical Angle } (\theta_c): \quad \boxed{\sin\theta_c = \frac{\mu_{\text{rarer}}}{\mu_{\text{denser}}} = \frac{1}{\mu}}$$
  • Condition for TIR: (1) Light must travel from a denser medium to a rarer medium ($\mu_1 > \mu_2$), and (2) Angle of incidence in the denser medium must exceed critical angle ($i > \theta_c$).
  • Optical Fibers: Core of refractive index $\mu_1$ surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index $\mu_2$ (${\mu_1 > \mu_2}$). Light undergoes repeated TIR with zero energy loss.
  • Radius of Bright Circle (Illuminated Disk) Seen from Underwater: A diver or fish looking upward sees all outside world light compressed inside a circular cone of semi-vertical angle equal to $\theta_c$:
    $$\boxed{R = h \tan\theta_c = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Illuminated Bright Circular Radius R = h / √(μ² − 1) Underwater

For a point light source at depth $h$ underwater (refractive index $\mu$), rays striking the surface at angle of incidence $i = \theta_c$ refract at $r = 90^\circ$ and skim along the water surface. From geometry, $\tan\theta_c = \frac{R}{h}$. Since $\sin\theta_c = \frac{1}{\mu} \implies \tan\theta_c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}$:

$$\boxed{R = h \tan\theta_c = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Frequency Does NOT Change During Refraction): When light passes from air into glass, its speed ($v = c/\mu$) and wavelength ($\lambda = \lambda_0/\mu$) both decrease by a factor of $\mu$, but its frequency $f$ (and color) remains 100% unchanged because frequency is determined strictly by the light source!

topics.title: Refraction at Curved Spherical Surfaces, Lens Maker's Formula, Thin Lens Combination & Silvered Lens
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Refraction at a Single Spherical Surface & Lens Maker's Formula
$$\text{Single Spherical Surface:} \quad \boxed{\frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}}$$
Lens Maker's Formula:
For a thin lens of refractive index $\mu_{\text{lens}}$ placed in a medium of refractive index $\mu_{\text{medium}}$ (with radii of curvature $R_1$ and $R_2$):
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{f} = \left({}^{\text{medium}}\mu_{\text{lens}} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right) = \left(\frac{\mu_{\text{lens}}}{\mu_{\text{medium}}} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)}$$
  • Lens Immersed in a Liquid of Higher Refractive Index ($\mu_L > \mu_{\text{lens}}$): The focal length changes sign! A convex converging lens in air becomes diverging in water (and vice versa)!
  • Combination of Two Thin Lenses in Contact: $\boxed{\frac{1}{F_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} \implies P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2}$.
3.2 Silvered Lens (Equivalent Mirror Power Formula)

When one surface of a lens of focal length $f_L$ is silvered, it acts as a single equivalent mirror of focal length $F_{\text{eq}}$:

$$\frac{1}{F_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{2}{f_L} + \frac{1}{f_M} \qquad \left(\text{where } f_M \text{ is the focal length of the equivalent mirror formed by the other silvered surface}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Lens Maker's Formula

Apply single spherical surface refraction twice: first surface gives $\frac{\mu_2}{v_1} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R_1}$. Second surface (with image $v_1$ acting as virtual object $u = v_1$ in medium $\mu_2$ going into $\mu_1$): $\frac{\mu_1}{v} - \frac{\mu_2}{v_1} = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{R_2}$. Adding the two equations and setting $u = -\infty, v = f$ yields the Lens Maker's Formula.

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap (Cutting a Lens):
    • Cutting a convex lens horizontally (parallel to principal axis): Focal length remains unchanged ($f' = f$), but intensity of image drops (less light gathered).
    • Cutting a convex lens vertically (perpendicular to principal axis into two symmetric halves): Focal length doubles ($f' = 2f$) for each half because each half now has one flat surface ($R_2 = \infty$).

topics.title: Refraction Through a Prism, Angle of Deviation (δ), Minimum Deviation, Optical Instruments (Simple & Compound Microscopes, Astronomical Telescope)
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Refraction Through a Glass Prism
$$\text{1. Master Prism Equations:} \quad \boxed{r_1 + r_2 = A} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{i + e = A + \delta}$$

Minimum Deviation (${\delta_{\min}}$): Occurs symmetrically when $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. Substituting into Snell's Law at the second surface gives:

$$\boxed{\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_{\min}}{2}\right)}{\sin(A/2)}} \qquad \left(\text{For a Thin Prism } (A \le 10^\circ): \quad \delta = A(\mu - 1)\right)$$
4.2 Optical Instruments: Microscopes & Telescopes
Optical InstrumentMagnifying Power (MP) FormulaNormal Adjustment Condition ($v_e = \infty$)
1. Simple Microscope (Magnifying Glass)$$\boxed{m = 1 + \frac{D}{f}}$$$$m_{\text{normal}} = \frac{D}{f} \quad (D = 25\text{ cm})$$
2. Compound Microscope (Objective $f_o$, Eyepiece $f_e$)$$m = -\frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$$$$\boxed{m_{\text{normal}} \approx -\frac{L}{f_o}\frac{D}{f_e}} \quad (L \approx v_o)$$
3. Astronomical Telescope (Objective $f_o$, Eyepiece $f_e$)$$m = -\frac{f_o}{u_e}$$$$\boxed{m_{\text{normal}} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}} \qquad (\text{Length } L = f_o + f_e)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Prism Refractive Index via Minimum Deviation

At minimum deviation $\delta = \delta_{\min}$, $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. The deviation angle is $\delta_{\min} = i + e - A = 2i - A \implies i = \frac{A + \delta_{\min}}{2}$. Applying Snell's Law $\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r_1}$ yields $\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_{\min}}{2}\right)}{\sin(A/2)}$$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Condition for Emergence from a Prism): For light to successfully emerge out of the second face of a prism without undergoing total internal reflection, the prism angle $A$ must be strictly less than $2\theta_c$ ($A < 2\theta_c$). If $A > 2\theta_c$, light is trapped inside!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 22: Ray Optics! Next, in Chapter 23, we explore wave interference and diffraction.
summary:
• Mirrors & Lenses: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$; Lens Maker $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
  • Refraction & TIR: $\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$; $\sin\theta_c = \frac{1}{\mu}$; Underwater disk $R = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}$.
  • Prism: $\mu = \frac{\sin((A+\delta_{\min})/2)}{\sin(A/2)}$; Thin prism $\delta = A(\mu - 1)$.
  • Instruments: Microscope $m \approx -\frac{L}{f_o}\frac{D}{f_e}$; Telescope $m = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$.
formulaSheetHtml:
ConceptMaster FormulaKey Notes
Lens Maker's Formula$\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{\mu_{\text{lens}}}{\mu_{\text{med}}} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$Convex in denser liquid becomes diverging.
Critical Angle & Radius$\sin\theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu}, \qquad R = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}$TIR requires denser to rarer medium.
Prism Min Deviation$\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_{\min}}{2}\right)}{\sin(A/2)}$At min dev, $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$.
Telescope Normal Adj.$m = -\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}, \qquad L = f_o + f_e$Objective focal length $f_o$ is very large.

questions.prompt: A concave mirror has a focal length of $f = -20\text{ cm}$. An object is placed at a distance $u = -30\text{ cm}$ in front of the mirror. Where is the image formed, and what is its magnification $m$?
questions.explanation: Using $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} \implies \frac{1}{-20} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-30} \implies \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-3 + 2}{60} = -\frac{1}{60} \implies v = -60\text{ cm}$. Magnification $m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-60}{-30} = -2$ (real and inverted).

questions.prompt: The refractive index of glass is $\mu = 1.5$. What is the critical angle $\theta_c$ for light traveling from glass into air? ($\arcsin(2/3) \approx 41.8^\circ$)
A equiconvex lens of refractive index $\mu = 1.5$ has a focal length of $f = 20\text{ cm}$ in air. What is the radius of curvature $R$ of each of its spherical surfaces?
questions.explanation: For an equiconvex lens, $R_1 = +R$ and $R_2 = -R$. Using Lens Maker's Formula: $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{-R}\right) = (1.5 - 1)\left(\frac{2}{R}\right) = \frac{1}{R} \implies R = f = 20\text{ cm}$.

questions.prompt: A ray of light passes through an equilateral glass prism ($A = 60^\circ$) such that the angle of incidence $i$ is equal to the angle of emergence $e$. If the angle of deviation is $\delta = 30^\circ$, what is the refractive index $\mu$ of the prism material?
questions.explanation: Since $i = e$, the ray undergoes minimum deviation: $\delta_{\min} = 30^\circ$. Using $\mu = \frac{\sin((A+\delta_{\min})/2)}{\sin(A/2)} = \frac{\sin((60^\circ+30^\circ)/2)}{\sin(60^\circ/2)} = \frac{\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1/2} = \sqrt{2}$.

questions.prompt: An astronomical telescope has an objective lens of focal length $f_o = 100\text{ cm}$ and an eyepiece of focal length $f_e = 5\text{ cm}$. When adjusted for normal adjustment, what is (i) the magnifying power $m$, and (ii) the length $L$ of the telescope tube?
questions.explanation: In normal adjustment, $m = -\frac{f_o}{f_e} = -\frac{100}{5} = -20$, and length $L = f_o + f_e = 100 + 5 = 105\text{ cm}$.

questions.prompt: A point light source is placed at a depth $h = 3\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}$ below the surface of a large tank of water (refractive index $\mu = 3/2$). A circular opaque disk of radius $R$ is placed floating on the water surface right above the source such that no light emerges out into the air from the water surface. What is the minimum radius $R$ of the disk?
questions.explanation: The radius of the illuminated circle is $R = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}$. To block all light, the floating disk must have a radius at least equal to $R$: $R_{\min} = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{(3/2)^2 - 1}} = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{9/4 - 1}} = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}/2} = 3 \times 2 = 6\text{ cm}$.
